body.text: Russia’s experience shows that building effective drone capabilities requires quality as much as quantity, a lesson India’s Integrated Battle Groups will need to consider as they prepare for sustained operations

In a recent incisive and insightful analysis of the battle tank’s relevance in ground operations, an Indian expert highlighted the significance of Persistent Robotic Overwatch (PRO. PRO is vital to the tank’s defence, as passive protection in the form of armour enhancements and Active Protection Systems (APS) is effective only up to a point and cannot defend against a saturated airborne drone attack.

Since variants of Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) are cheap to produce and deploy, crewed armoured vehicles are particularly vulnerable. The tank’s organic ability to defend against anti-tank munitions has reached its limits: it cannot be packed with too much armour, nor can it be equipped with APS to defend against kinetic projectiles and intense drone assaults beyond a point. As a result, the PRO is required to protect the crewed tank against incoming anti-tank munitions by creating a layered defensive bubble. Most crucially, the PRO is also expected to aid the offence. The supply of munitions, the flow of crew and unmanned systems will need to exceed whatever India’s twin adversaries — China and Pakistan — can amass and deploy. This PRO, as some have contended, should be along the lines of the Russian Rubicon units. Although the latter have not been fully developed, have continued to evolve, or have been used effectively, they provide a template for the Indian Army’s (IA) extant and evolving IBGs.
The real test, as the Russian experience suggests, is the imperative to exploit and create offensive breakthroughs.

The succeeding analysis evaluates the requirements for an Indian PRO capability. Indeed, the Indian Army (IA)’s Integrated Battle Groups (IBGs) already possess some of the accoutrements of Russia’s Rubicon units. The real test, as the Russian experience suggests, is the imperative to exploit and create offensive breakthroughs. The Indian expert’s contention is apt; however, it does not fully consider two issues — the objectives of armour-laden IBGs equipped with a PRO bubble for offensive action and the manpower required, both in qualitative and quantitative terms, to generate a territorial breakthrough.

The Indian expert evaluating Russian Rubicon units has not fully considered the quality of manpower necessary to sustain this prescription for a PRO capability. This brings us to the composition of the Russian Rubicon units and whether these units can serve as a template for shaping and strengthening India’s IBGs.

In 2024-25, the Russian Rubicon Center was established with the explicit purpose of serving as an overarching organisation responsible for “research, procurement, training and operational deployment.” The scope of its mandate is fairly expansive and also includes doctrinal development covering tactics, techniques and procedures (TTPs). It was initially meant to be a centralised entity to render Russian drone production capabilities more scalable. The deployment of these unmanned systems is designed to be seamless in key areas across the battlefront, with the Rubicon Center serving as the link between its unmanned developmental initiatives and their battlefield deployment. The Center seeks to integrate and employ AI-enabled unmanned systems for battlefield operations.
However, this expansion has not been without challenges. Most critically, human talent is a constraint.

In terms of personnel, Rubicon expanded its personnel strength across its specialised combat units. These units included a wide range of First-Person-View (FPV) quadcopters and reconnaissance systems such as the Orlan-10 and Supercam, as well as Counter-Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (C-UAV) and electronic warfare squads. In March 2025, the Rubicon Center had a total of roughly 1,450 personnel, with a sanctioned limit of 2,500 personnel. By the first quarter of 2026, Rubicon had roughly 9,000 personnel.

However, this expansion has not been without challenges. Most critically, human talent is a constraint. The Center started recruiting experienced UAS teams from its conventional formations, which depleted their capabilities in Intelligence, Surveillance and Reconnaissance (ISR) and fire support for Russian ground units. The Rubicon Center is also in competition with the 50th Unmanned Systems Brigade (USB), which is itself expanding from 1,300 personnel to 7,000 personnel. In total, the Unmanned Systems Forces had roughly 87,000 personnel, with plans to increase this to 165,000 personnel by the end of 2026. At present, Russia is unable to meet its monthly recruitment targets.

Consequently, the Russians have been compelled to lower their recruitment standards to meet their quotas. Meeting quantitative benchmarks too rapidly has undermined quality. A similar pattern emerged in Ukraine when the country expanded the size of its drone line regiments and brigades too quickly, temporarily weakening their capabilities. Further, the demand for and scarcity of quality manpower is a product of Russia’s expansive military objectives and the resulting prolonged military campaign — both of which constrain its ability to recruit high-quality personnel. Therefore, the attrition suffered by Russian forces among their UAS and C-UAS teams has not been easily replaced.
What Rubicon Means for India’s IBGs

The Russian experience, and to some extent the Ukrainian experience, is instructive for India’s IBGs facing China and Pakistan. Any “PRO bubble” India develops as an integral part of its IBGs will need to take into account the scope of the IA's objectives against China and Pakistan, as well as the commensurate demands these will place on personnel and the unmanned systems India will deploy.

Escalation is a two-way street. China’s PLA Ground Force (PLAGF) and Pakistan Army (PA) can also expand the conflict area against India and pursue offensive action. Thus, the duration of any war with either China or Pakistan, or both, will not be entirely within the IA’s control, as Russia’s experience in Ukraine demonstrates. The IA’s IBGs will therefore sustain a PRO for both offensive and defensive missions. If India pursues more offensive action, it will require greater exertion and, commensurately, greater investment by the IA in a PRO capability.
The PRO bubble will matter as much for defensive IBG operations requiring a reserve capability as it would for offensive action.

The PRO bubble will matter as much for defensive IBG operations requiring a reserve capability as it would for offensive action. Since defence tends to be stronger in war than offence, defensive, armour-intensive IBG manoeuvre operations are likely to place more limited demands on the PRO bubble. For armour-intensive offensive manoeuvre operations that will underpin the IBGs against a two-front military threat, the means required will be substantial, as will the attrition they suffer. To be sure, the latter can be stronger and more effective if the IBGs’ defences are under considerable stress and pressure, or when a tactical deadlock needs to be broken. Indeed, offensive armour-intensive IBG operations are imperative if the purpose is to secure a territorial quid pro quo as the IA did during the 1965 India-Pakistan war.

To support the IBGs' rapid response, high-tempo operations, providing personnel of sufficient quality and quantity at scale will be as important as magazine depth and drone manufacturing capabilities with Artificial Intelligence (AI) augmentation. Indeed, Russia’s experience in the ongoing war is a lesson the IA will need to imbibe when structuring the IBGs, but tailored to the IA’s military objectives, supported by technical manpower, application of emerging technologies, skilled drone operators and India’s military-industrial strength.
